title: Isu Specialty Chemical to Start Korea's First Commercial Lithium Sulfide Production in October
content:
Korea Supply Chain Brief · September 29, 2026

Isu Specialty Chemical will start commercial production of lithium sulfide — the core raw material for sulfide-based solid-state batteries — at its Ulsan plant in the fourth week of October, ahead of every other Korean lithium sulfide maker. Here is why this material is the bottleneck for solid-state batteries, how Isu says it will cut the price, and what happens next.

CompanyRoleEvidence
Isu Specialty Chemical
(Isu Group affiliate)		First mover to commercial-scale lithium sulfide production in KoreaExclusive report (Korea Economic TV, Sep 29, 2026)
Lake MaterialsAlso building lithium sulfide capacity; still at the sample-evaluation stageReported
Samsung SDIExpected to be the first Korean battery maker to commercialize solid-state batteries, starting next yearReported

What was reported

  • Startup timing: commercial production begins in the fourth week of October at the Ulsan plant, which was completed in June and has since been in trial operation and quality-stabilization testing.
  • Initial capacity: 150 tons per year, with plans to expand to as much as 500 tons.
  • Customer activity: Isu is beginning deliveries to customers while running additional sample testing with about 10 companies in Korea, China, and Japan.
  • This year's sales estimate: around 20 tons of lithium sulfide, since the plant only starts up in late October — meaning this year's financial impact is limited, but next year's is the one to watch if sample tests convert to supply contracts.
  • Company financials (2026 estimate): revenue of KRW 427 billion and operating profit of KRW 26.7 billion, driven mainly by recovering prices and higher utilization in its existing precision chemicals business — with lithium sulfide commercialization layered on top going forward.

Why lithium sulfide is the bottleneck material

Lithium sulfide is the key raw material for sulfide-based solid-state batteries, which promise lower fire risk and longer range per charge than today's batteries — a combination seen as suited not only to electric vehicles but to humanoid robots that need to operate for long stretches. Korean battery makers, having lost ground in LFP batteries to Chinese rivals, are treating solid-state technology as their next-generation edge, with Samsung SDI expected to be the first to commercialize it starting next year. But the report says lithium sulfide today costs around $700 per kilogram because manufacturing is difficult and no one has reached mass-production scale — making raw-material supply the actual constraint on how fast solid-state batteries can commercialize.

How Isu says it will cut the price

Isu's approach is a "continuous process," as opposed to the standard "batch process" used elsewhere, where raw materials are loaded and processed one batch at a time. In a continuous process, material flows from input to finished product without stopping, allowing larger, more stable volumes per run and, Isu says, a lower per-unit cost. The company also has a raw-material advantage: lithium sulfide requires lithium and hydrogen sulfide, and hydrogen sulfide is highly toxic and difficult to source or transport externally. Isu Specialty Chemical can draw hydrogen sulfide as a byproduct from its affiliate Isu Chemical's own chemical production, rather than sourcing it externally.

How Isu compares to rivals, per the report

  • Lake Materials: has also built lithium sulfide production facilities but remains at the sample-evaluation stage, behind Isu on commercial timing.
  • Chinese producers: the industry view cited in the report is that Chinese lithium sulfide technology still contains more impurities than Korean producers' output.

Isu has participated in government-backed national research projects since 2020 and holds nine patents from that work. Its Ulsan plant also received loan support from the government's national growth fund, and the report frames the government's recent push to cultivate solid-state battery technology and localize key battery materials as a tailwind for the company.

What is not disclosed

  • Which specific companies are among the roughly 10 running sample tests with Isu.
  • Whether any sample test has converted, or is expected to convert, into a signed supply contract.
  • Isu Specialty Chemical's listing status or ticker — this brief does not confirm whether the company is separately listed from its parent group.

Quick FAQ

What is lithium sulfide used for?
It is the core raw material for sulfide-based solid-state batteries, a next-generation battery technology aimed at electric vehicles and humanoid robots.

When does Isu Specialty Chemical start commercial production?
The fourth week of October, at a Ulsan plant completed in June, with initial capacity of 150 tons per year and a plan to scale to 500 tons.

Why is lithium sulfide expensive today?
It costs around $700 per kilogram because manufacturing is difficult and no producer has reached mass-production scale yet, according to the report.

How is Isu trying to lower costs?
Through a continuous manufacturing process instead of a batch process, and by sourcing hydrogen sulfide, a hazardous raw material, as a byproduct from its affiliate Isu Chemical rather than externally.
